I'll bite on why Mint is a pain in the ass, even though I'm not grandparent (though I am great-grandparent!).

Mint is fantastic if you stay within the sandbox it gives you. If you need to recompile a package (say, making pulseaudio only talk to JACK), Mint starts showing warts.

Eventually, the advanced Mint/Ubuntu/Debian user starts getting frustrated enough by the limitations of the package manager that they start maintaining their own custom source builds in a separate directory (~/local/src or /usr/src are two common locations). At that point, the AUR starts to look a little more enticing.

In cases like mine (I went from Redhat 4.2 to Mandrake 6.0 to Gentoo), it was building GNOME 0.98.x betas and Enlightenment DR 0.15 betas simultaneously from CVS twice a week (on a Pentium 133MHz!) that made a binary package manager frustrating. Gentoo, outside the week-long learning curve of "why doesn't my monolithic kernel boot?", has been a fantastic friend to me these long years. It's kept my systems secure, my house warm, my house security working, and has literally kept me out of jail in one instance in 2016. I make it mandatory on any system I'm paid to work on or babysit. Everyone else gets Mint, because I'll only have to look at it once every two years to do a system upgrade, and the only reason it breaks is if they have an Nvidia card, and the driver didn't rebuild with a kernel update.

TL;DR - Mint is fantastic until you start getting tangled in the soft safety net they give you.
